topics.title: Intro CP 3.27
topics.text:
I have 7 different keys: 2 for my house, 2 for my car, 3 for my office. I want to place the keys in a keyring such that the house keys are next to each other and the car keys are next to each other. In how many ways can I place keys on the keyring?



Why is my solution wrong?

Solution:

Treat house, car and office keys as 1 block each. There are $3!$ ways to arrange the block. Within each block, there are $2!, 2!, 3!$ ways to organize the house, car and office keys respectively. So we have $3! \cdot 3! \cdot 2! \cdot 2!$. Dividing by $3\cdot 2$ for rotation and flipping symmetry, gives us $24$ possibilities.

If the coordinate of one point of a triangle is $A=(0,0)$, another is $B=(2b, 2c)$, and a third is $C=(2a, 0)$, prove that the centroid of the triangle splits each median in a $1:2$ ratio using coordinate bashing.



My workWe designate the midpoint of $\overline{AC}$ $E=(a,0)$, and the midpoint of $\overline{BC}$ $D=(a+b, c)$. We know that if we can find the equations of $\overline{BE}$ and $\overline{AD}$, then we can find the intersection of the lines and then find the equation of the third median so that we can prove all three medians intersect the centroid.



The point-slope formula for finding the equation of a line is $y-m=\frac{y_1-y_2}{x_1-x_2}x-b$. Thus, the equation of $\overline{BE}$ is $y=\frac{2c}{a-2b}x-a$. Furthermore, the equation of $\overline{AD}$ is $y=\frac{c}{a+b}x$. We equate them together and get $\frac{2c}{a-2b}x-a=\frac{c}{a+b}x$. Now I am stuck. topics.title: How To Divide In Modular Arithmetic
topics.text:
Many people have questions regarding modular division. Here is how you divide in modular arithmetic:



[quote=Summary Of Useful Facts from AoPS Intro to Modular Arithmetic Wiki Page]Division: $a\equiv b \pmod m \implies \frac{a}{\gcd (a,b)}\equiv \frac{b}{e}\pmod {\frac{m}{\gcd(m,\gcd (a,b))}}$, where $e$ is a positive integer that divides ${a}$ and $b$.[/quote]



Note that in this rule, it is convenient to choose $e$ to be as large as possible to simplify the congruence as much as possible. The maximum possible value of $e$ is $e=\gcd(a,b)$. Try out examples to make sure you understand this concept. For practice, go to this website: http://www.dcode.fr/modular-equation-solver and practice solving modular congruences with a coefficient greater than 1, by creating your own.



Many people say that you just multiply by the modular inverse instead of division, but what if the modular inverse is undefined? Modular division is then the best way to go.



[quote=WARNING from Volume 1]Division does not work in the regular way in modular congruences.[/quote]

topics.title: Mathcounts mini 2009 Sequences Problem
topics.text:
The arithmetic progressions ${2,5,8,11...}$ and ${3,10,17,24...}$ have some common values. What is the largest value less than 500 that they have in common?

Solution:

Click to reveal hidden textWe apply the arithmetic sequence formula to get that the first sequence can be displayed as the following:

$a_n=2+3(n-1)$ or $a_n=3n-1$. We convert the second one into $a_n=3+7(x-1)$ or $a_n=7x-4$. We notice that they are equal, so we make en equations setting them equal:

$3n-1=7x-4$.

I combine the constants to derive: $3n+3=7x$.

Now, here comes the part I am not sure of.

I factor a 3 out of the expression to get $3(n+1)=7x$. By this factoring, would it be correct to say that $x$ is divisible by $3$?

I made this assumption and found the largest number that was satisfied my criteria. I plugged in $69$ for $x$ and found $479$ to be the largest value. Is my assumption correct?
